notes.definition: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, such as uranium or plutonium, into two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, releasing two or three neutrons, gamma rays and energy.
explanation: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239. Spontaneous fission (splitting without any outside cause) is rare. Usually, for fission to occur, the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. For example, a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a slow-moving neutron and becomes uranium-236, which is very unstable and splits almost immediately.

When the nucleus splits, it forms two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, and also emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays. Energy is released by the fission reaction. All of the fission products (the two smaller nuclei and the neutrons) have kinetic energy, and the gamma rays carry energy away too. A typical example is: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n. As in all nuclear equations, the mass numbers and atomic numbers balance.

The neutrons released can go on to be absorbed by other uranium nuclei, causing them to split and release more neutrons. This is called a chain reaction. If every fission caused two more fissions, the number of fissions would double each step: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on, releasing energy very quickly.

In a nuclear reactor, the chain reaction is controlled so that energy is released at a steady rate. Control rods, made of a material such as boron that absorbs neutrons, are raised or lowered into the reactor core. Lowering them absorbs more neutrons, so fewer fissions happen and less energy is released. A moderator (such as graphite or water) slows the neutrons down so that they are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 nuclei. The energy released heats water to make steam, which turns turbines to generate electricity. On average, exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission.

The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction. The number of fissions increases extremely rapidly, so a huge amount of energy is released in a fraction of a second. You should be able to draw and interpret diagrams showing a neutron being absorbed, the nucleus splitting into two daughter nuclei and neutrons, and those neutrons going on to cause further fissions.
keyFacts: Fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus such as uranium or plutonium.
Spontaneous fission is rare; usually the nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size.
Two or three neutrons and gamma rays are also emitted.
Energy is released; all fission products have kinetic energy.
Released neutrons can cause further fissions: a chain reaction.
In a reactor the chain reaction is controlled (control rods absorb neutrons) so energy is released steadily.
A nuclear weapon explosion is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.
Mass numbers and atomic numbers balance in fission equations.

keyTerms.definition: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, with the release of neutrons, gamma rays and energy.
Fission that happens without the nucleus first absorbing a neutron; it is rare.
A reaction in which neutrons released by fission cause further fissions, which release more neutrons.
The two smaller (daughter) nuclei and neutrons produced in fission, all of which have kinetic energy.
Rods that absorb neutrons; moved into or out of a reactor core to control the rate of fission.
A material in a reactor that slows neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 nuclei.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fission happens when a neutron hits a nucleus hard enough to smash it apart.
misconceptions.right: In fact the nucleus absorbs the neutron, becomes unstable and then splits. Slow neutrons are more likely to be absorbed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse fission with fusion.
misconceptions.right: In fact fission is splitting a large nucleus; fusion is joining two light nuclei.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think control rods slow neutrons down.
misconceptions.right: In fact control rods absorb neutrons. The moderator slows them down.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a nuclear reactor could explode like a nuclear bomb.
misconceptions.right: In fact a reactor's chain reaction is controlled. A bomb needs an uncontrolled chain reaction in highly concentrated fissile material.

realWorld: Nuclear power stations in the UK generate a significant share of the country's electricity using fission of uranium-235.
Some submarines and aircraft carriers are powered by small fission reactors, so they can travel for years without refuelling.
Fission products such as caesium-137 make used reactor fuel highly radioactive, so it must be stored and cooled carefully.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only. It is not assessed in Combined Science Trilogy (8464).
examTips: Describe fission in order: neutron absorbed, nucleus becomes unstable, splits into two smaller nuclei, releases 2 or 3 neutrons, gamma rays and energy.
In diagrams, show the neutrons from one fission going on to be absorbed by other nuclei to show a chain reaction.
Remember: control rods absorb neutrons; moderators slow them down.
To balance fission equations, add the neutron on the left to the uranium mass number before subtracting.
summary: Fission splits a large unstable nucleus (uranium or plutonium) into two smaller nuclei.
Usually a neutron must be absorbed first; spontaneous fission is rare.
Two or three neutrons, gamma rays and energy are released; all products have kinetic energy.
Released neutrons can cause a chain reaction.
Reactors control the chain reaction; nuclear weapons use an uncontrolled one.

questions.question: What is nuclear fission?
options: Splitting a large unstable nucleus into smaller nuclei
A nucleus emitting an alpha particle
markScheme: 1 mark: Splitting a large unstable nucleus into smaller nuclei
questions.explanation: Fission means splitting. Joining small nuclei is fusion, and alpha emission is radioactive decay.

questions.question: Which of these is commonly used as a fuel in fission reactors?
markScheme: 1 mark: Uranium
questions.explanation: Uranium (and plutonium) are large unstable nuclei that can undergo fission. Hydrogen is used in fusion.

questions.question: What must usually happen to a uranium-235 nucleus before it undergoes fission?
markScheme: 1 mark: It must absorb a neutron
questions.explanation: Spontaneous fission is rare. Usually the nucleus absorbs a neutron, becomes unstable and splits.

questions.question: How many neutrons are typically released in each fission of uranium-235?
markScheme: 1 mark: Two or three
questions.explanation: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons, which can go on to cause further fissions.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a nuclear reactor.
What is the job of the control rods in the nuclear reactor?
options: To absorb neutrons and control the rate of fission
To carry heat to the turbines
markScheme: 1 mark: To absorb neutrons and control the rate of fission
questions.explanation: Control rods absorb neutrons. Lowering them reduces the number of fissions. The moderator slows neutrons.

questions.question: What causes the explosion of a nuclear weapon?
options: Spontaneous fission of a single nucleus
markScheme: 1 mark: An uncontrolled chain reaction
questions.explanation: In a weapon, the number of fissions grows extremely quickly in an uncontrolled chain reaction.

questions.question: Which statement about the two nuclei produced in fission is correct?
options: They are roughly equal in size
One is always a helium nucleus
They are larger than the original nucleus
markScheme: 1 mark: They are roughly equal in size
questions.explanation: Fission produces two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, and all fission products have kinetic energy.

questions.question: Control rods are lowered further into a reactor core. What happens?
options: More neutrons are absorbed, so fewer fissions occur and less energy is released
Neutrons are slowed down, so more fissions occur
More neutrons are released, so more energy is released
markScheme: 1 mark: More neutrons are absorbed, so fewer fissions occur and less energy is released
questions.explanation: Lower rods absorb more neutrons, so fewer are available to cause fission. The reaction slows and the power output falls.

questions.question: In a reactor running at a steady rate, on average how many neutrons from each fission go on to cause another fission?
markScheme: 1 mark: Exactly one
questions.explanation: If exactly one neutron per fission causes another fission, the rate stays constant. More than one would make it grow; fewer would make it die out.

questions.question:
The equation shows the fission of a uranium-235 nucleus.
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n
Determine the value of x.
markScheme: 1 mark: x = 3
questions.explanation: Left: 235 + 1 = 236. Right: 141 + 92 = 233, so 3 neutrons.

questions.question:
The equation shows the fission of a uranium-235 nucleus.
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + 2 ¹₀n
The xenon nucleus has an atomic number of 54 and a mass number of A.
Determine the value of A.
markScheme: 1 mark: A = 140
questions.explanation: Include the incoming neutron on the left (236) and the two outgoing neutrons on the right.

questions.question:
The equation shows the fission of a uranium-235 nucleus.
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → Cs + ⁹⁶₃₇Rb + 3 ¹₀n
The caesium nucleus has a mass number of 137 and an atomic number of Z.
Determine the value of Z.
markScheme: 1 mark: 92 = Z + 37 (neutrons have atomic number 0)
1 mark: Z = 55
questions.explanation: Neutrons carry no charge, so the atomic numbers of the two nuclei add up to 92.

In this chain reaction each fission causes 2 further fissions.
Step 1 is a single fission.
Calculate the number of fissions in step 10.
markScheme: 1 mark: number in step n = 2⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾

questions.explanation: Step 1 = 1, step 2 = 2, step 3 = 4 ... step 10 = 2⁹ = 512. A common error is 2¹⁰ = 1024.

Figure 1 shows a uranium-235 nucleus undergoing fission.
The nucleus splits into two daughter nuclei.
Name particle X and radiation Y, which are also released.

1 mark: Y: gamma rays

questions.question: State what is meant by spontaneous fission.
markScheme: 1 mark: fission that happens without the nucleus absorbing a neutron (it splits by itself)
questions.explanation: Spontaneous fission is rare; most fission is induced by neutron absorption.

questions.question: Describe what happens when a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission.
markScheme: 1 mark: nucleus absorbs a neutron (and becomes unstable U-236)
1 mark: splits into two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size
1 mark: releases 2 or 3 neutrons, gamma rays and energy
questions.explanation: Describe the sequence in order for full marks.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a chain reaction.
Explain how a chain reaction happens.
markScheme: 1 mark: each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons
1 mark: these are absorbed by other uranium nuclei, causing further fissions (which release more neutrons)
questions.explanation: The released neutrons are what keep the reaction going.

questions.question: Explain the difference between the chain reaction in a nuclear reactor and in a nuclear weapon.
markScheme: 1 mark: in a reactor the chain reaction is controlled so energy is released at a steady rate
1 mark: in a weapon it is uncontrolled so the number of fissions increases rapidly and energy is released in an explosion
questions.explanation: Control is the key difference.

questions.question: Explain why a moderator is needed in a nuclear reactor.
acceptedAnswers: slow neutrons more likely to be absorbed
markScheme: 1 mark: it slows down the neutrons released by fission
1 mark: slow neutrons are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 nuclei, so fission continues
questions.explanation: Fast neutrons are less likely to be absorbed, so the chain reaction could stop.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a nuclear reactor.
Suggest what would happen to the chain reaction in the reactor if all the control rods were removed.
Explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: fewer neutrons would be absorbed, so more neutrons cause fission
1 mark: the rate of fission and energy release would increase rapidly (the reactor could overheat)
questions.explanation: Control rods keep the number of neutrons causing fission at about one per fission.

questions.question: What is released when a large nucleus undergoes fission?
markScheme: 1 mark: Energy, neutrons and gamma rays
questions.explanation: Fission releases two smaller nuclei, 2 or 3 neutrons, gamma rays and energy.

questions.question: What is the role of the moderator in a nuclear reactor?
options: To absorb neutrons and stop the reaction
To shield workers from gamma rays
To slow neutrons down so they are more likely to cause fission
markScheme: 1 mark: To slow neutrons down so they are more likely to cause fission
questions.explanation: The moderator slows neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods.

questions.question: Which nucleus can undergo fission in a nuclear reactor?
markScheme: 1 mark: Plutonium-239
questions.explanation: Plutonium-239, like uranium-235, is a large unstable nucleus that can split. Light nuclei such as hydrogen and helium are involved in fusion, not fission.

questions.question: Describe the process of nuclear fission of uranium-235 and explain how a chain reaction can occur. You may include a labelled diagram.
markScheme: Indicative content: neutron absorbed by uranium-235 nucleus; nucleus becomes unstable; splits into two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size; releases 2 or 3 neutrons, gamma rays and energy; fission products have kinetic energy; released neutrons absorbed by other U-235 nuclei; cause further fissions; chain reaction; diagram showing neutrons from one fission causing more fissions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear sequence of fission and a correct explanation of how the neutrons lead to a chain reaction.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description of splitting or of a chain reaction.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The link between released neutrons and further fissions is the key to a chain reaction.

questions.question: Explain how energy is released in a nuclear reactor and how the rate of energy release is controlled. Include a description of fission, the role of the control rods and the moderator, and why a reactor does not explode like a nuclear weapon.
markScheme: Indicative content: uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a slow neutron; becomes unstable and splits into two smaller nuclei plus 2 or 3 neutrons and gamma rays; energy released, products have kinetic energy; this heats the reactor core and coolant; heat used to make steam for turbines and generator; moderator slows neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed; control rods absorb neutrons; lowering rods reduces number of fissions, raising them increases it; steady rate when on average one neutron per fission causes another fission; weapon uses an uncontrolled chain reaction where number of fissions grows rapidly; reactor is controlled so this does not happen.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered explanation covering fission, energy transfer, moderator, control rods, steady chain reaction and the contrast with a weapon.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes fission and at least one control method with some explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about fission or reactors.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Separate the roles clearly: moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb them; control keeps the chain reaction steady.
